1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling, authorization
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked by `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This is a language-model review grounded by a static scanner (semgrep) and by this program's mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`); it is not a certification of security.
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so semgrep was run: `semgrep --config <local code-safety pack> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat` (72 files tracked by git scanned, 113 rules, 29 findings, 10 non-fatal parse errors on files outside this department's scope). Every semgrep hit was treated only as a place to read, never as a finding on its own. The one access-relevant hit — six `express-cookie-settings` sub-rules firing on the same `express-session(...)` call at `server.js:78-102` (no name, no httpOnly, no secure, no domain, no path, no expires) — was independently read in full and is reported below. The remaining hits (NoSQL `$where` injection in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, `eval()` on request input in `app/routes/contributions.js`, `code-string-concat` on the same lines, an open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72`, plaintext-HTTP links in the tutorial HTML pages, hardcoded secrets in `config/env/*.js`, and mutable GitHub Actions tags) belong to the injection, platform, secrets, and dependencies departments and are not re-reported here; they were read only far enough to confirm they are not themselves the access-control gap on their route.
8: 
9: Route table built by reading every handler registered in `app/routes/index.js` (the sole place routes are mounted, plus the router it delegates to) and the full middleware chain in front of each, then reading every handler function itself:
10: 
11: | Route | Method | Registration | Middleware chain | Handler read |
12: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
13: | `/` | GET | index.js:30 | none | session.js `displayWelcomePage` — redirects to `/login` if no session |
14: | `/login` | GET/POST | index.js:33-34 | none | session.js `displayLoginPage` / `handleLoginRequest` |
15: | `/signup` | GET/POST | index.js:37-38 | none | session.js `displaySignupPage` / `handleSignup` |
16: | `/logout` | GET | index.js:41 | none | session.js `displayLogoutPage` — calls `req.session.destroy()`, correctly ends the session |
17: | `/dashboard` | GET | index.js:44 | `isLoggedIn` | session.js `displayWelcomePage` |
18: | `/profile` | GET/POST | index.js:47-48 | `isLoggedIn` | profile.js — scoped to `req.session.userId`, not attacker-controlled |
19: | `/contributions` | GET/POST | index.js:51-52 | `isLoggedIn` | contributions.js — scoped to `req.session.userId` |
20: | `/benefits` | GET/POST | index.js:55-56 | `isLoggedIn` only (`isAdmin` middleware exists at index.js:27 but is never attached; the fix is commented out at index.js:57-60) | benefits.js — **finding below** |
21: | `/allocations/:userId` | GET | index.js:63 | `isLoggedIn` | allocations.js — **finding below**, `:userId` taken from the URL, not the session |
22: | `/memos` | GET/POST | index.js:66-67 | `isLoggedIn` | memos.js — a single shared memo list with no per-user scoping by design, not an IDOR |
23: | `/learn` | GET | index.js:70-73 | `isLoggedIn` | open redirect via `req.query.url` — injection/platform territory, not reported here |
24: | `/research` | GET | index.js:76 | `isLoggedIn` | research.js — SSRF via `req.query.url` — injection territory |
25: | `/tutorial/*` | GET | index.js:79 → tutorial.js:8-37 | none | static tutorial pages, no state change, out of scope |
26: 
27: For every route above, an unauthenticated caller (no `req.session.userId`) is redirected to `/login` by `isLoggedIn` or `isAdminUserMiddleware` (both read in full, `app/routes/session.js:25-42`), except `/`, `/login`, `/signup`, `/logout`, and `/tutorial/*`, which are intentionally public. The gap this review found is not at that layer: `isLoggedIn` only proves *some* valid session exists, so a caller authenticated as the wrong identity — any ordinary, non-admin account — still passes it cleanly on `/benefits` (no role check at all) and on `/allocations/:userId` (no ownership check against the requested id), which is where the two authorization findings below live.
28: 
29: Files read in full: `server.js`, `config/config.js`, `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`, `app/routes/allocations.js`, `app/routes/benefits.js`, `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/memos.js`, `app/routes/research.js`, `app/routes/tutorial.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`. Files read in part to confirm a handler's data flow (DAO layer, invoked from the routes above): `app/data/profile-dao.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`, `app/data/allocations-dao.js`.
30: 
31: ## Findings
32: 
33: 1. **`access-idor-allocations-userid`** (high, confirmed, CWE-639) — `GET /allocations/:userId` (`app/routes/index.js:63`) checks only that the caller is logged in; the handler trusts `req.params.userId` (`app/routes/allocations.js:16-18`, with the correct fix visible but commented out immediately above it) and hands it straight to the DAO with no ownership check, so any account can read any other user's allocation data.
34: 2. **`access-missing-admin-check-benefits`** (high, confirmed, CWE-862) — `POST /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:56`, same gap on the paired `GET` at line 55) never applies the `isAdmin` middleware that already exists and works (`app/routes/session.js:25-34`); any logged-in user can overwrite another user's `benefitStartDate` and view the admin roster.
35: 3. **`access-login-no-session-regenerate`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-384) — `handleLoginRequest` sets `req.session.userId` (`app/routes/session.js:116`) without regenerating the session id first, unlike `handleSignup` in the same file, which calls `req.session.regenerate()` before doing the same assignment (line 234); a session id fixed before login carries the victim's post-login privileges.
36: 4. **`access-password-compare-not-constant-time`** (high, confirmed, CWE-916) — `comparePassword` (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`) is a plain `fromDB === fromUser`, timing-unsafe, comparing against a password that is never hashed in the first place (`user-dao.js:25`, with `bcrypt.hashSync` commented out at line 29).
37: 5. **`access-csrf-missing-profile-update`** (high, confirmed, CWE-352) — `csurf()` is never mounted anywhere in `server.js` (commented out at line 7 and again at lines 104-113); `POST /profile` (`app/routes/index.js:48`) accepts bank account, routing, SSN, and address changes from a cookie-only session with no token check anywhere.
38: 6. **`access-session-cookie-insecure-config`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-614 / CWE-1004) — the `express-session` call (`server.js:78-102`) sets no `cookie` block at all: no `httpOnly`, no `secure`, no `maxAge`, confirmed both by reading the object literal and by six semgrep `express-cookie-settings` sub-rules firing on the same span.
39: 
40: ## What was not covered
41: 
42: - **Injection-adjacent issues visible in the same files were left to the injection department**: the NoSQL `$where` query in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78`, the `eval()` on `req.body.preTax/afterTax/roth` in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, the open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72` (`/learn`), and the SSRF in `app/routes/research.js:14-16`. These were read enough to confirm they are not themselves the access-control gap on those routes (each route's `isLoggedIn` check is present and correct), not traced end-to-end for their own sinks.
43: - **Hardcoded secrets** (`config/env/all.js:8`, `config/env/development.js:6`, `config/env/test.js:6`) were located via semgrep and are a secrets-department finding; the cookie-signing secret's exposure bears on session integrity but the finding itself — a committed literal — is theirs to report, not duplicated here.
44: - **MFA** — NodeGoat has no MFA implementation anywhere in the files read; there is nothing to evaluate for CWE-308, so no finding was written for it.
45: - **Brute-force protection on `/login` and `/signup`** — no rate limiter or lockout middleware is registered anywhere in `server.js` or `app/routes/index.js` (`package.json` has no `express-rate-limit`-style dependency, and no manual attempt-counting appears in `session.js`). This is a real gap, but it was not written up as a numbered finding because no single line registers the (absent) control to quote against the "quote the exact line" rule; it is recorded here as a gap the customer's own team should close, most naturally by adding a per-account limiter in front of `app.post("/login", sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest)` at `app/routes/index.js:34`.
46: - **View-layer files** (`app/views/*.html`) were not read for access-control issues such as whether admin-only UI elements are merely hidden client-side rather than enforced server-side; the two routes flagged above (finding 1 and finding 2) make this concern moot for `/benefits` and `/allocations`, but the remaining views were not audited for the same pattern.
47: - **`test/`, `artifacts/`, and asset/vendor files** were not read; they carry no route registrations and are out of this department's scope.
48: - **JWT** — NodeGoat's session layer uses `express-session` cookie sessions on every route read, not JWTs; the JWT-pitfalls portion of the access skill does not apply to this codebase and was not evaluated further.
49: 
50: ## Certificate
51: 
52: `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/access.json` was run after writing this file and reported all six findings verified against the locked target tree.
53: 
54: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

(End of file - total 54 lines)
</content>

`semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so semgrep was run: `semgrep --config <local code-safety pack> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat` (72 files tracked by git scanned, 113 rules, 29 findings, 10 non-fatal parse errors on files outside this department's scope). Every semgrep hit was treated only as a place to read, never as a finding on its own. The one access-relevant hit — six `express-cookie-settings` sub-rules firing on the same `express-session(...)` call at `server.js:78-102` (no name, no httpOnly, no secure, no domain, no path, no expires) — was independently read in full and is reported below. The remaining hits (NoSQL `$where` injection in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, `eval()` on request input in `app/routes/contributions.js`, `code-string-concat` on the same lines, an open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72`, plaintext-HTTP links in the tutorial HTML pages, hardcoded secrets in `config/env/*.js`, and mutable GitHub Actions tags) belong to the injection, platform, secrets, and dependencies departments and are not re-reported here; they were read only far enough to confirm they are not themselves the access-control gap on their route.

Route table built by reading every handler registered in `app/routes/index.js` (the sole place routes are mounted, plus the router it delegates to) and the full middleware chain in front of each, then reading every handler function itself:
| Route | Method | Registration | Middleware chain | Handler read |
| `/` | GET | index.js:30 | none | session.js `displayWelcomePage` — redirects to `/login` if no session |
| `/logout` | GET | index.js:41 | none | session.js `displayLogoutPage` — calls `req.session.destroy()`, correctly ends the session |
| `/profile` | GET/POST | index.js:47-48 | `isLoggedIn` | profile.js — scoped to `req.session.userId`, not attacker-controlled |

| `/benefits` | GET/POST | index.js:55-56 | `isLoggedIn` only (`isAdmin` middleware exists at index.js:27 but is never attached; the fix is commented out at index.js:57-60) | benefits.js — **finding below** |
| `/allocations/:userId` | GET | index.js:63 | `isLoggedIn` | allocations.js — **finding below**, `:userId` taken from the URL, not the session |
| `/memos` | GET/POST | index.js:66-67 | `isLoggedIn` | memos.js — a single shared memo list with no per-user scoping by design, not an IDOR |
| `/learn` | GET | index.js:70-73 | `isLoggedIn` | open redirect via `req.query.url` — injection/platform territory, not reported here |
| `/research` | GET | index.js:76 | `isLoggedIn` | research.js — SSRF via `req.query.url` — injection territory |
| `/tutorial/*` | GET | index.js:79 → tutorial.js:8-37 | none | static tutorial pages, no state change, out of scope |

For every route above, an unauthenticated caller (no `req.session.userId`) is redirected to `/login` by `isLoggedIn` or `isAdminUserMiddleware` (both read in full, `app/routes/session.js:25-42`), except `/`, `/login`, `/signup`, `/logout`, and `/tutorial/*`, which are intentionally public. The gap this review found is not at that layer: `isLoggedIn` only proves *some* valid session exists, so a caller authenticated as the wrong identity — any ordinary, non-admin account — still passes it cleanly on `/benefits` (no role check at all) and on `/allocations/:userId` (no ownership check against the requested id), which is where the two authorization findings below live.

Files read in full: `server.js`, `config/config.js`, `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`, `app/routes/allocations.js`, `app/routes/benefits.js`, `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/memos.js`, `app/routes/research.js`, `app/routes/tutorial.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`. Files read in part to confirm a handler's data flow (DAO layer, invoked from the routes above): `app/data/profile-dao.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`, `app/data/allocations-dao.js`.

1. **`access-idor-allocations-userid`** (high, confirmed, CWE-639) — `GET /allocations/:userId` (`app/routes/index.js:63`) checks only that the caller is logged in; the handler trusts `req.params.userId` (`app/routes/allocations.js:16-18`, with the correct fix visible but commented out immediately above it) and hands it straight to the DAO with no ownership check, so any account can read any other user's allocation data.

2. **`access-missing-admin-check-benefits`** (high, confirmed, CWE-862) — `POST /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:56`, same gap on the paired `GET` at line 55) never applies the `isAdmin` middleware that already exists and works (`app/routes/session.js:25-34`); any logged-in user can overwrite another user's `benefitStartDate` and view the admin roster.

3. **`access-login-no-session-regenerate`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-384) — `handleLoginRequest` sets `req.session.userId` (`app/routes/session.js:116`) without regenerating the session id first, unlike `handleSignup` in the same file, which calls `req.session.regenerate()` before doing the same assignment (line 234); a session id fixed before login carries the victim's post-login privileges.

4. **`access-password-compare-not-constant-time`** (high, confirmed, CWE-916) — `comparePassword` (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`) is a plain `fromDB === fromUser`, timing-unsafe, comparing against a password that is never hashed in the first place (`user-dao.js:25`, with `bcrypt.hashSync` commented out at line 29).

5. **`access-csrf-missing-profile-update`** (high, confirmed, CWE-352) — `csurf()` is never mounted anywhere in `server.js` (commented out at line 7 and again at lines 104-113); `POST /profile` (`app/routes/index.js:48`) accepts bank account, routing, SSN, and address changes from a cookie-only session with no token check anywhere.

6. **`access-session-cookie-insecure-config`** (medium, confirmed, CWE-614 / CWE-1004) — the `express-session` call (`server.js:78-102`) sets no `cookie` block at all: no `httpOnly`, no `secure`, no `maxAge`, confirmed both by reading the object literal and by six semgrep `express-cookie-settings` sub-rules firing on the same span.

- **Injection-adjacent issues visible in the same files were left to the injection department**: the NoSQL `$where` query in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78`, the `eval()` on `req.body.preTax/afterTax/roth` in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, the open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72` (`/learn`), and the SSRF in `app/routes/research.js:14-16`. These were read enough to confirm they are not themselves the access-control gap on those routes (each route's `isLoggedIn` check is present and correct), not traced end-to-end for their own sinks.

- **Hardcoded secrets** (`config/env/all.js:8`, `config/env/development.js:6`, `config/env/test.js:6`) were located via semgrep and are a secrets-department finding; the cookie-signing secret's exposure bears on session integrity but the finding itself — a committed literal — is theirs to report, not duplicated here.
- **MFA** — NodeGoat has no MFA implementation anywhere in the files read; there is nothing to evaluate for CWE-308, so no finding was written for it.

- **Brute-force protection on `/login` and `/signup`** — no rate limiter or lockout middleware is registered anywhere in `server.js` or `app/routes/index.js` (`package.json` has no `express-rate-limit`-style dependency, and no manual attempt-counting appears in `session.js`). This is a real gap, but it was not written up as a numbered finding because no single line registers the (absent) control to quote against the "quote the exact line" rule; it is recorded here as a gap the customer's own team should close, most naturally by adding a per-account limiter in front of `app.post("/login", sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest)` at `app/routes/index.js:34`.

- **View-layer files** (`app/views/*.html`) were not read for access-control issues such as whether admin-only UI elements are merely hidden client-side rather than enforced server-side; the two routes flagged above (finding 1 and finding 2) make this concern moot for `/benefits` and `/allocations`, but the remaining views were not audited for the same pattern.
- **`test/`, `artifacts/`, and asset/vendor files** were not read; they carry no route registrations and are out of this department's scope.

- **JWT** — NodeGoat's session layer uses `express-session` cookie sessions on every route read, not JWTs; the JWT-pitfalls portion of the access skill does not apply to this codebase and was not evaluated further.
`node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/access.json` was run after writing this file and reported all six findings verified against the locked target tree.

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

37:   Signup writes `req.body.password` straight into the MongoDB user document;
38:   the `bcrypt.hashSync` call that would hash it is commented out, and
39:   `validateLogin`'s `comparePassword` (line 61) does a raw `===` string
40:   compare against the stored value, confirming it is never hashed. A database
41:   read of any kind (backup, admin, injection, stolen credential) yields every
42:   user's real login password.

46: - **`data-hardcoded-cookie-secret`** (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798) — The
47:   express-session signing secret is the literal

49:   Anyone with the source can forge a valid session cookie for any user id.
50: - **`data-config-logged-at-startup`** (`config/config.js:12-13`, CWE-532) —
51:   `console.log(util.inspect(config, false, null))` dumps the entire merged

86: - **Dependencies and known-CVE packages** (e.g. `bcrypt-nodejs`, `swig`,

89:   dead code (see `data-plaintext-password-storage`).
90: - **Session cookie flags** (`httpOnly`, `secure`, `maxAge` on
91:   `server.js:78-102`) and **CSRF** — left to the `access` department, which
92:   owns session management; not reported here to avoid duplicate findings
93:   on the same lines under a different CWE.
94: - **NoSQL injection** in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78` and the
95:   `eval`-adjacent string concatenation in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`
96:   (both flagged by semgrep) — read only far enough to see they are injection
97:   sinks, not data-exposure sinks; left to the `injection` department.
98: - **`app/routes/{allocations,memos,research,tutorial}.js`** and the
99:   corresponding DAOs beyond `benefits-dao.js`/`contributions-dao.js` were
100:   skimmed for obvious logging/PII sinks but not traced end to end; no
101:   additional sensitive-data sink was found there, but this was not an
102:   exhaustive read.
103: - **Runtime/deployment configuration** — whether a reverse proxy in front of
104:   this app terminates TLS in the actual deployment, what log
105:   aggregator (if any) receives the stdout that `data-config-logged-at-startup`
106:   writes to, and what `MONGODB_URI` is actually set to in production are
107:   outside what a static read of this repository can confirm.
108: - **Timing side channels** in the plaintext `===` password comparison
109:   (`user-dao.js:61`) were not analyzed separately; the plaintext-storage
110:   finding already covers the root cause.

1: # Injection and traversal — NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, read-only for this review; nothing was written into the target tree). This is a language-model review grounded by a static scanner and by the mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`).
6: 
7: `semgrep 1.177.0` was available and was run from the target root with both the local pack (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep`) and the registry pack `p/owasp-top-ten` (the registry was reachable, so both packs ran together, `--metrics off`). It reported 29 raw hits across 113 rules over 72 git-tracked files. Every hit was treated as a place to read, not as a finding: several (GitHub Actions mutable tags, cookie-setting defaults, plaintext HTTP links in tutorial prose) belong to other departments (platform/dependencies) and are out of scope here; the injection-relevant hits (`$where` in `allocations-dao.js`, `eval` and string concatenation in `contributions.js`, the open redirect in `index.js`) were each read in full, in the surrounding handler and DAO, before being written up.
8: 
9: Following the review-method discipline, every route registered in `app/routes/index.js` and `app/routes/tutorial.js` was read first, then each handler was traced forward into its DAO and its template. Read in full: `server.js` (template-engine and session setup), `app/routes/*.js` (all eight route modules), `app/data/*.js` (all seven DAOs), and the views whose controllers pass request-derived data into them (`memos.html`, `profile.html`, `allocations.html`, `research.html`). `config/config.js` and `config/env/*.js` were read to confirm which values are environment-derived versus literal.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: Nine findings, all `confirmed` — the tainted source, every intermediate function, and the sink were read for each, with no sanitizer or framework guard in between.
14: 
15: ### Critical
16: 
17: - **`injection-eval-pretax`**, **`injection-eval-aftertax`**, **`injection-eval-roth`** — `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`. `POST /contributions` passes `req.body.preTax`, `req.body.afterTax` and `req.body.roth` straight into `eval()`, three separate calls, three separate sinks. Validation (`isNaN`/negative checks) runs only after `eval` has already executed. Any authenticated user can run arbitrary JavaScript in the server process — full remote code execution, not merely a query- or markup-level injection. Fix: replace each `eval(...)` with `Number(...)`/`parseInt(...)` plus a `NaN` check, exactly as the disabled fix already commented into the same file demonstrates.
18: 
19: ### High
20: 
21: - **`injection-nosql-where-allocations`** — `app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`. `threshold` flows unvalidated from `GET /allocations/:userId?threshold=...` (`app/routes/allocations.js:20`) into a MongoDB `$where` clause built by template-literal interpolation, letting an attacker run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server (denial of service, or reading other users' allocation data by injecting an always-true expression). Fix: bound-check `threshold` as an integer and use a plain query object (`{ userId, stocks: { $gt: threshold } }`), never a `$where` string, matching the disabled fix already present in the file.
22: - **`injection-ssrf-research`** — `app/routes/research.js:16`. `GET /research` concatenates `req.query.url` and `req.query.symbol` — both fully attacker-controlled query parameters, the form's hidden `url` field only pre-fills the browser UI and is not enforced server-side — into a URL handed to `needle.get()`, and the fetched body is written back to the client raw. An attacker can point this at an internal address or a cloud metadata endpoint and read the response through the app. Fix: allowlist the destination host, block private/link-local/metadata ranges, and re-check the resolved IP before the request.
23: - **`injection-xss-memos-marked`** — `app/views/memos.html:31`. `req.body.memo` is stored unsanitized (`app/data/memos-dao.js`) and rendered through `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}` with swig's `autoescape` globally disabled (`server.js:137`); the only remaining guard is `marked`'s own deprecated, bypassable `sanitize: true` option. Any logged-in user can plant markup that executes in every other viewer's browser when they open `/memos`. Fix: re-enable swig autoescaping and sanitize the rendered HTML with an allowlist library (e.g. DOMPurify) immediately before the raw-output sink.
24: 
25: ### Medium
26: 
27: - **`injection-open-redirect-learn`** — `app/routes/index.js:72`. `GET /learn` redirects to `req.query.url` with no allowlist or relative-path check — a classic open-redirect usable for phishing from a trusted NodeGoat link. Fix: allowlist destination hosts/paths or restrict to relative, in-application paths.
28: - **`injection-xss-profile-firstname-value`** and **`injection-xss-profile-firstname-href`** — `app/views/profile.html:41` and `:78`. When the profile-update form's bank-routing regex rejects a submission, `app/routes/profile.js:64` echoes `req.body.firstName` back unencoded as `firstNameSafeString`, which two separate template sinks place — once inside an `value` attribute, once inside an `href` attribute (as a `javascript:` URI) — with swig autoescaping disabled. Each is a distinct sink an attacker can trigger independently (attribute breakout vs. `javascript:` scheme). Fix: re-enable autoescaping, and for the `href` context specifically, URL-encode into a separate field as the code's own `@FIXME` comment already prescribes.
29: 
30: ## What was not covered
31: 
32: - **Client-side JavaScript and the bundled vendor libraries** (`app/assets/vendor/*`, `app/assets/js/*`) were not reviewed for DOM-based sinks (`innerHTML`, `document.write`); these are third-party or non-request-driven assets and were out of scope for this pass.
33: - **`app/assets/js/tour/redirects-steps.js`** and the tutorial content pages (`app/views/tutorial/*.html`) were skimmed for structure but not traced line-by-line; they are static walkthrough pages, not live request handlers, except where `tutorial.js` renders them by a fixed, hardcoded page list (`app/routes/tutorial.js:15-28`), which is not attacker-influenced and was not written up.
34: - **CSRF, session-cookie flags, and authentication/authorization logic** (e.g. `app/routes/session.js`'s login/signup flow, the missing `isAdmin` check on `/benefits`) are access-control and session-management concerns, not injection, and are left to the `access` department; they were read only far enough to confirm they don't also constitute an injection sink.
35: - **Dependency-level vulnerabilities** (e.g. the pinned `marked@0.3.5`, whose `sanitize` option is deprecated in later releases and was never a complete HTML sanitizer) are named here only as forming part of the `memos.html` finding's evidence; a full advisory lookup against `package.json`/`package-lock.json` is the `dependencies` department's job and was not performed.
36: - **Runtime/deployment configuration** — actual environment variables, reverse-proxy or WAF rules, and whether `NODE_ENV=production` changes any of the behaviors above — was not available to a static read and is not confirmed either way.
37: - No SQL findings are reported because NodeGoat has no relational-database layer; all persistence is through the MongoDB driver, covered under the NoSQL/`$where` finding above.

(End of file - total 37 lines)
</content>

`dsh-hardcoded-secret` rule plus the `p/owasp-top-ten` registry pack) was run over
the target tree and every hit was read and manually confirmed before being kept or
dropped. The review covered configuration, startup/seed scripts, the active
application routes, CI files, and the Dockerfile; it did not cover git history (no
`.git` directory is in the locked scope) or third-party dependency advisories.
The target is read-only; nothing was written into it. Tooling: `semgrep 1.177.0`
was run with `--config <local fixtures>/semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off
--json .` over the target root (the registry pack was reachable, so both rule sets
ran together, 113 rules over 72 git-tracked files, 29 raw hits). Every semgrep hit
was treated strictly as a place to read, never as a finding on its own; each was
opened and traced by hand. Method otherwise follows the review-method skill: entry
points and config loaders read first (`server.js`, `config/config.js`,
`config/env/*.js`), then each candidate secret traced forward to where — if
anywhere — it is actually consumed by the running service, and one finding written
per sink with the exact line quoted and a stated confidence level. Files read in

- `secrets-cookie-secret` — Express session signing secret is hard-coded in the committed default configuration (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798, confirmed) — a public, unrotated HMAC key for every session cookie; fix by reading it from a required environment variable and rotating.

- `secrets-admin-default-credential` — Admin account is seeded with a hard-coded plaintext password compared in cleartext (`artifacts/db-reset.js:18`, CWE-798, confirmed) — remote login as `admin`/`Admin_123` on any default deployment; fix by generating a random admin password at first run and storing only its bcrypt hash.

- `secrets-config-console-log` — Full application config, including the session secret and crypto key, is written to stdout on every boot (`config/config.js:12-13`, CWE-532, confirmed) — both secrets land in every container/process log; fix by removing the dump or redacting known-sensitive keys before logging.

- `secrets-crypto-key-unused-config` — A hard-coded AES/PBKDF2 key is committed, though the code that would consume it is currently commented out (`config/env/all.js:9`, CWE-321, confirmed) — dead today, but the published key would immediately be in production use for SSN/DOB encryption if the documented fix were re-enabled; fix by sourcing it from a secrets manager or removing the dead field.

- `secrets-tls-private-key-committed` — An RSA private key is committed to the repository and referenced only by a commented-out HTTPS listener (`artifacts/cert/server.key:1`, CWE-321, confirmed) — every clone already holds the key; fix by never shipping a private key in source and rotating this one.

- `secrets-zap-api-key-dev-config` — OWASP ZAP proxy API key for local security-scan tooling is hard-coded in the development config (`config/env/development.js:6`, CWE-798, confirmed) — authenticates only to a private-range lab host, not a production credential; fix by moving it to an environment variable read by the test harness.

- `secrets-admin-credential-e2e-fixture` — Cypress e2e fixture repeats the seeded admin password in plaintext (`test/e2e/fixtures/users/admin.json:3`, CWE-798, confirmed) — test-only copy of the live finding `secrets-admin-default-credential`, reported at lower severity because it is not itself wired into the running service; fix follows once the live credential is rotated.

- Git history: the locked target tree excludes `.git`, so no full-history secret scan (gitleaks/trufflehog) was run; a secret rotated in the working tree could still be reachable in an earlier commit and this review cannot confirm either way.
- Third-party dependency advisories (`package.json`/`package-lock.json` contents) — out of scope for this department, covered separately by the dependencies department.

- Runtime/deployed configuration: actual environment-variable values used in any real deployment of this app, Heroku config vars implied by `app.json`, or any secret manager that might already front `MONGODB_URI` in a real environment — none of that is visible from a static read of the source tree.

- `test/security/profile-test.js:37` (`sutUserPassword = "User1_123"`) and the remaining `test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json` files were read and confirmed to repeat the same seeded test-user password already covered by `secrets-admin-default-credential`'s sibling accounts in `artifacts/db-reset.js`; they were not filed as separate findings to avoid padding the count with duplicates of an already-reported root cause.
- Binary/minified vendor assets under `app/assets/vendor/` were not opened; they are third-party libraries, not this application's configuration or secrets.

`node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/secrets.json` mechanically confirmed that all 7 findings resolve to an existing file and line (ignoring only whitespace) in the locked target tree, that all 7 ids are unique, and that no two findings share file, line, and CWE.

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

content.text:
### critical

- `data-plaintext-password-storage` — User passwords are stored in MongoDB as plaintext, not hashed (`app/data/user-dao.js:25`, CWE-256, confirmed) — Anyone who reads the users collection - a database backup, an admin, a NoSQL-injection read, or a compromised DB credential - obtains every user's real login password in cleartext, directly reusable against this and any other site the user reused it on. Hash the password with bcrypt (or argon2id) before insert, e.g. `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync(12))`, and compare with bcrypt.compareSync in validateLogin instead of `===`.
- `dependencies-swig-unmaintained-file-read` — swig, the active template engine, is deprecated/unmaintained and has an unfixed arbitrary local file read advisory (`package.json:22`, CWE-22, confirmed) — Combined with any template-injection path, an attacker can read arbitrary files on the server filesystem; there is no upstream fix and the maintainers have stopped shipping one, so this risk is permanent as long as swig stays in the dependency tree. Replace swig with a maintained template engine (the project already loads templates through `consolidate`, which supports several current engines), and re-enable autoescaping in whatever engine replaces it.
- `dependencies-underscore-rce` — underscore is pinned to a range resolving to a version with a known arbitrary-code-execution advisory (`package.json:23`, CWE-94, confirmed) — If `_.template` is ever called with attacker-influenced template source or options, an attacker can execute arbitrary code in the Node.js process; independently, a crafted deeply-nested object handed to `_.flatten` or `_.isEqual` can crash the process via stack exhaustion. Update underscore to >=1.13.8 and confirm no code path in the application passes attacker-controlled strings into `_.template`.
- `injection-eval-pretax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (preTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:32`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can submit a POST /contributions request with preTax set to arbitrary JavaScript (e.g. `require('child_process').execSync('id')` or a process-crashing payload) and have it executed in the Node process, giving full server-side code execution under the application's privileges. Never eval request data. Parse the value with Number()/parseInt() and reject non-numeric input, as the commented-out fix in the same file (lines 37-40) already shows.
- `injection-eval-aftertax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (afterTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:33`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting afterTax to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution. Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) plus a NaN check before use.
- `injection-eval-roth` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (roth) (`app/routes/contributions.js:34`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting roth to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution. Replace eval(req.body.roth) with Number(req.body.roth) or parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) plus a NaN check before use.

### high

- `access-idor-allocations-userid` — Allocations route is an IDOR: any logged-in user can read any other user's allocation data by editing the URL (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, confirmed) — Any authenticated low-privilege user can walk the numeric :userId path segment (e.g. /allocations/1, /allocations/2, ...) and receive another user's stock/fund/bond allocation data. Ignore the :userId route parameter and load allocations for req.session.userId only, or verify req.session.userId === req.params.userId (or that the caller is admin) before calling the DAO.
- `access-missing-admin-check-benefits` — Admin-only benefits routes have no role check; any logged-in user can view and overwrite any other user's benefit start date (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, confirmed) — Any authenticated non-admin user can POST an arbitrary userId and benefitStartDate to overwrite another employee's benefits record, and can view the admin benefits roster of all non-admin users -- a full vertical privilege escalation on a state-changing route. Add the existing isAdmin middleware to both routes exactly as the commented-out code shows: app.get("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...) and app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...).
- `access-password-compare-not-constant-time` — Login compares passwords with plain string equality on plaintext-stored passwords instead of a constant-time hash verify (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-916, confirmed) — The === comparison leaks timing information proportional to the number of matching leading characters, letting an attacker who can measure response time recover a valid password character-by-character; independently, because passwords are stored in plaintext, any read access to the users collection discloses every user's real password in the clear, not a hash. Hash passwords on signup with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())) and verify with the library's constant-time bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) instead of ===.
- `access-csrf-missing-profile-update` — No CSRF protection anywhere in the app: profile update (bank account, SSN, address) is forgeable from a cookie-authenticated session (`app/routes/index.js:48`, CWE-352, confirmed) — A page on another origin that auto-submits a form to POST /profile (the victim's session cookie is attached automatically by the browser) can silently overwrite the victim's bank account number, routing number, SSN, address, and name. Re-enable csurf() (or an equivalent double-submit/SameSite=Strict scheme) mounted before the routes in server.js, and include the token in every state-changing form (profile, benefits, contributions, memos, login).
- `data-config-logged-at-startup` — Full application config, including session secret and crypto key, is dumped to stdout on every start (`config/config.js:12-13`, CWE-532, confirmed) — Anyone who can read the process's stdout/log files - container logs, a log-aggregation pipeline, a support engineer, or an attacker with log read access - obtains the session-signing secret, the crypto key, and the database credentials in one line, enough to forge sessions for any user and to connect to the database directly. Remove the startup config dump, or log an explicit allowlist of non-secret fields (e.g. port, hostName) instead of the whole object.
- `data-cleartext-pii-storage` — SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are stored in MongoDB unencrypted (`app/data/profile-dao.js:55-66`, CWE-312, confirmed) — Anyone who reads the users collection - a database backup, an admin, an SSRF/NoSQL-injection read path, or a stolen DB credential - obtains every user's real SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers in cleartext. Re-enable field-level encryption (AES-256-GCM with a random IV per record, key from a vault) before writing ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting, and decrypt only when displaying to the owning user.
- `data-cleartext-http-transport` — Application only listens over plain HTTP; TLS is fully disabled (`server.js:145`, CWE-319, confirmed) — Any attacker positioned on the network path (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP, or a man-in-the-middle) can read or modify login credentials, session cookies and all submitted PII in transit. Terminate TLS at the app or a reverse proxy in front of it, redirect all HTTP to HTTPS, and set the session cookie's `secure` flag once TLS is in place.
- `dependencies-express-outdated-vulnerable` — express is a vulnerable 4.x release pulling six vulnerable transitive packages (`package.json:13`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — An attacker can redirect users to attacker-controlled hosts, inject markup via response.redirect(), or trigger denial-of-service through the vulnerable transitive qs/path-to-regexp parsers -- reachable on every request the framework handles, unauthenticated. Update express to >=4.21.2 (still within the declared ^4.13.4 range; `npm audit fix` reports a fix is available without a manifest change) and regenerate package-lock.json so the transitive body-parser/cookie/qs/send/serve-static versions are refreshed too.
- `dependencies-body-parser-dos` — body-parser is pinned to a range that resolves to a version with two denial-of-service advisories (`package.json:9`, CWE-405, confirmed) — An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted request body to exhaust event-loop time or bypass the configured body-size limit, denying service to the whole application. Update body-parser to >=1.20.6 (within the declared ^1.15.1 range; npm audit reports a non-breaking fix is available) and regenerate the lockfile.
- `dependencies-marked-xss-redos` — marked is pinned to an exact, years-old version with active XSS and ReDoS advisories, and is wired into templates (`package.json:17`, CWE-79, confirmed) — A user who can submit markdown content (e.g. via the memos feature) can bypass marked's sanitize option and inject script that executes in another user's session, or trigger a ReDoS that stalls the single Node.js event loop for every request. At minimum update to marked@0.3.19 (the non-major fix npm audit resolves within this branch); for a durable fix, migrate off the deprecated `sanitize` option entirely and run output through a maintained HTML sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify) on a current marked major version.
- `dependencies-mongodb-driver-outdated` — mongodb driver is pinned to an ancient 2.x range with a DoS advisory and an unmaintained transitive driver-core (`package.json:18`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — A malformed server response or crafted query result can crash or hang the database connection layer that every route in the application depends on; the 2.x driver also predates years of TLS, authentication and query-hardening fixes shipped in later majors. At minimum update to mongodb >=3.1.13 to clear the known DoS; plan a migration to a current major (7.x) since the 2.x line is long past any security support window.
- `injection-nosql-where-allocations` — NoSQL injection via unsanitized threshold in MongoDB $where clause (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`, CWE-943, confirmed) — An attacker can submit GET /allocations/<userId>?threshold=' ; while(true){} // or an operator such as 0' ; return true; var x='0 to run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server, causing denial of service or bypassing the intended filter to read every user's allocation data. Never build a $where clause from request input. Validate `threshold` as a bounded integer (parseInt with a 0-99 range check, as the commented-out original fix does) and use a plain query object such as { userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } } instead of a $where string.
- `injection-ssrf-research` — Server-side request forgery via unvalidated url/symbol query parameters (`app/routes/research.js:16`, CWE-918, confirmed) — An authenticated user can set url to an internal or cloud-metadata address (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/ or http://localhost:<internal-port>/) and have the server fetch it on their behalf, exfiltrating internal service responses or cloud credentials back through the reflected response body. Validate and allowlist the destination host (e.g. restrict to finance.yahoo.com) before calling needle.get, resolve and re-check the IP to block private/link-local/metadata ranges, and never let the request supply the full request URL.
- `injection-xss-memos-marked` — Stored XSS: unescaped markdown-rendered memo output with autoescape disabled (`app/views/memos.html:31`, CWE-79, confirmed) — Any logged-in user can submit a memo containing HTML/script content (e.g. via a markdown construct marked's sanitizer fails to strip, or raw HTML since sanitize is not a full parser-level guarantee) that executes in every other user's browser when they view /memos, enabling session/cookie theft or actions performed as another user. Re-enable swig's default autoescaping (remove autoescape: false in server.js) and, for the deliberately-raw markdown output, sanitize the rendered HTML with an allowlist library (e.g. DOMPurify server-side) immediately before rendering rather than relying on marked's sanitize option alone.
- `platform-missing-security-headers` — No security response headers are set anywhere in the middleware stack (`server.js:68`, CWE-693, confirmed) — Clickjacking (no frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options), unrestricted script/style sources for any injected content (no CSP), MIME-type confusion attacks (no X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff), no forced HTTPS upgrade (no HSTS), and easy fingerprinting of the framework/version via X-Powered-By to target known Express/Node CVEs. Require and mount helmet() as the first middleware in the stack, before favicon/body-parser/session: `app.use(helmet());` plus an explicit `contentSecurityPolicy` policy, `app.disable("x-powered-by")`, and `helmet.hsts()` once the app is served over HTTPS.
- `platform-no-rate-limiting-auth` — Login and signup routes have no rate limiting or lockout (`app/routes/index.js:34`, CWE-307, confirmed) — An attacker can script unlimited username/password guesses against /login (and account-enumeration or spam signups against /signup at index.js:38) at whatever rate the network allows, making credential stuffing and brute force practical against any account. Mount a limiter (e.g. express-rate-limit) keyed by IP and by username/account on /login, /signup, and any password-reset route, with a lockout or exponential backoff after repeated failures.
- `secrets-cookie-secret` — Express session signing secret is hard-coded in the committed default configuration (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798, confirmed) — Anyone who has read the (public, OWASP-published) source tree knows the exact HMAC key express-session uses to sign the session-id cookie. They can craft or tamper with a session cookie's signature for any session id, which is the building block for session fixation/hijacking against any user of a deployment that has not overridden this default. Read the secret from a required environment variable (fail startup if unset) and generate a unique, random value per deployment; rotate the committed value since it must now be treated as burned.
- `secrets-admin-default-credential` — Admin account is seeded with a hard-coded plaintext password that the running app compares in cleartext (`artifacts/db-reset.js:18`, CWE-798, confirmed) — Anyone who has read this source (a public OWASP training repo) can log in as `admin`/`Admin_123` on any deployment that used the default seed, reaching the admin-only `/benefits` route (gated by `isAdminUserMiddleware` in app/routes/session.js) and every other authenticated user's data. Remove the hard-coded seed password from source; generate a random admin password at first-run time (or require an operator-supplied one via environment variable) and store only its bcrypt hash, using the already-present but commented-out bcrypt path.

### medium

- `access-login-no-session-regenerate` — Login does not regenerate the session id, allowing session fixation (`app/routes/session.js:116`, CWE-384, confirmed) — An attacker who fixes a victim's pre-login session id (trivial here since sessions exist for unauthenticated visitors too) inherits the victim's authenticated session once the victim logs in with that id, without ever seeing the victim's credentials. Call req.session.regenerate() before setting req.session.userId in handleLoginRequest, exactly as handleSignup already does.
- `access-session-cookie-insecure-config` — Session cookie is configured with no httpOnly, no secure flag, and no maxAge (never expires) (`server.js:78-102`, CWE-614, confirmed) — The session cookie is readable by any script injected via XSS (no httpOnly), is sent in the clear (no secure flag, plain HTTP server), and carries no explicit bound on its lifetime, so a stolen or fixed session id remains usable for as long as the session store keeps it alive. Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, maxAge: <a bounded value>, sameSite: 'lax' } in the session() call and serve over HTTPS.
- `data-hardcoded-crypto-key` — AES encryption key for PII is a hard-coded literal committed to source (`config/env/all.js:9`, CWE-798, confirmed) — If the intended SSN/DOB encryption were turned on, anyone with this committed key could decrypt every user's stored SSN and date of birth; today it also confirms the AES key an operator would need to reuse for any other encryption using this config. Load cryptoKey from environment/secret storage per deployment, generate it with a CSPRNG, and rotate the committed value.
- `data-pii-rendered-cleartext-to-client` — Profile page renders SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers in cleartext in the HTML response (`app/views/profile.html:49-61`, CWE-200, confirmed) — The user's SSN, date of birth and full bank account/routing numbers appear in plain text in the page's HTML source on every profile view - visible in browser history/cache, any proxy or corporate web-filter log, and to anyone positioned to read the unencrypted HTTP response (see data-cleartext-http-transport). Mask sensitive fields in the UI (e.g. show only the last 4 digits) and require a fresh, explicit reveal action; never place full SSN/bank numbers in a rendered form value.
- `dependencies-forever-transitive-prototype-pollution` — forever, a production dependency, pulls four vulnerable transitive packages including a prototype-pollution advisory in nconf (`package.json:15`, CWE-1321, confirmed) — forever itself is not on the HTTP request path, so the realistic exploitation route is through whatever configuration files or environment forever's own tooling parses via nconf; a prototype-pollution there could corrupt process-wide object behavior for anything else sharing the process. Bump the declared range to forever@^4.0.3 (a major upgrade, per npm audit's fixAvailable) or, given forever predates modern process supervisors, replace it with a maintained alternative such as pm2 or a systemd unit.
- `dependencies-bcrypt-nodejs-abandoned` — bcrypt-nodejs, the password-hashing library, is an npm-flagged deprecated package with no further releases (`package.json:8`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — The single component responsible for password hashing has no maintainer watching for weaknesses in its bcrypt implementation or new algorithmic guidance; any future flaw found in it will never receive an upstream patch. Migrate to the maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` (pure JS) package, as the deprecation notice itself recommends.
- `dependencies-grunt-env-floating-latest` — grunt-env is declared with the floating range "latest" instead of a pinned version (`package.json:50`, CWE-1357, confirmed) — A future malicious or simply breaking publish of grunt-env is installed automatically and silently, with no version bump or diff for reviewers to see in package.json; this is a supply-chain integrity gap independent of any currently known CVE. Pin grunt-env to an exact resolved version (matching what package-lock.json currently locks it to) and let dependabot/renovate propose bumps explicitly instead of floating to "latest".
- `dependencies-grunt-if-unpinned-git-tarball` — grunt-if is installed from a GitHub branch tarball with no tag or commit pin (`package.json:51`, CWE-829, confirmed) — Whatever the `master` branch of that third-party repository contains at install time runs in the build/test pipeline with no version pin or independent review step, and package-lock.json cannot meaningfully pin its content the way it does for registry packages. Replace the branch tarball reference with a pinned commit SHA or, preferably, a published, versioned release of grunt-if (or a maintained alternative) resolved through the npm registry.
- `injection-open-redirect-learn` — Open redirect via unvalidated url query parameter (`app/routes/index.js:72`, CWE-601, confirmed) — An attacker can craft a link such as /learn?url=https://evil.example/phish that, once clicked by a logged-in victim, redirects them from a trusted NodeGoat URL to an attacker-controlled site for phishing or credential harvesting. Validate the target against an allowlist of known learning-resource hosts/paths, or only allow relative paths within the application, before calling res.redirect().
- `injection-xss-profile-firstname-value` — Reflected XSS: unescaped firstName echoed into input value attribute (`app/views/profile.html:41`, CWE-79, confirmed) — A user can submit firstName containing `"><script>...</script>` in a POST /profile request with an intentionally-invalid bankRouting value, breaking out of the value attribute and executing arbitrary script in their own (or, if combined with another stored path, another user's) browser session. Enable swig's default autoescaping, or explicitly HTML-attribute-encode firstName (e.g. via node-esapi's encodeForHTMLAttribute, matching the pattern already used for `website` at profile.js:28) before assigning it to firstNameSafeString.
- `injection-xss-profile-firstname-href` — Reflected XSS: unescaped firstName echoed into href attribute (javascript: URI) (`app/views/profile.html:78`, CWE-79, confirmed) — A user can set firstName to `javascript:alert(document.cookie)` so that clicking the rendered 'Google search this profile by name' link executes arbitrary script in the victim's browser session, since the value lands directly in an href with no URL-context encoding or scheme allowlist. - `platform-error-handler-discloses-error` — Global error handler renders the raw error object into the HTML response with auto-escaping disabled (`app/views/error-template.html:11`, CWE-209, confirmed) — Any unhandled error anywhere in the request pipeline (DB errors, thrown exceptions from route handlers) is echoed to the client, leaking internal error text (library names, query context, file paths) that helps an attacker map the backend, and — because auto-escaping is off — any HTML/script characters the error text happens to contain would also be rendered unescaped. In errorHandler, render only a generic message and a correlation id to the client (`res.render("error-template", { error: "Something went wrong. Reference: " + reqId })`), keep the full message/stack in server-side logs only, and re-enable swig auto-escaping.

- `dependencies-node-esapi-abandoned` — node-esapi, used for output encoding, has had a single release since 2014 and no maintenance since (`package.json:20`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — A dependency chosen specifically for output-encoding correctness has had no bug fixes, no updates for newer encoding contexts, and no security review in over a decade; any encoding gap it has today will never be closed upstream. 4: - `data-plaintext-password-storage` — User passwords are stored in MongoDB as plaintext, not hashed (`app/data/user-dao.js:25`, CWE-256, confirmed) — Anyone who reads the users collection - a database backup, an admin, a NoSQL-injection read, or a compromised DB credential - obtains every user's real login password in cleartext, directly reusable against this and any other site the user reused it on. Hash the password with bcrypt (or argon2id) before insert, e.g. `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync(12))`, and compare with bcrypt.compareSync in validateLogin instead of `===`.
5: - `dependencies-swig-unmaintained-file-read` — swig, the active template engine, is deprecated/unmaintained and has an unfixed arbitrary local file read advisory (`package.json:22`, CWE-22, confirmed) — Combined with any template-injection path, an attacker can read arbitrary files on the server filesystem; there is no upstream fix and the maintainers have stopped shipping one, so this risk is permanent as long as swig stays in the dependency tree. Replace swig with a maintained template engine (the project already loads templates through `consolidate`, which supports several current engines), and re-enable autoescaping in whatever engine replaces it.
6: - `dependencies-underscore-rce` — underscore is pinned to a range resolving to a version with a known arbitrary-code-execution advisory (`package.json:23`, CWE-94, confirmed) — If `_.template` is ever called with attacker-influenced template source or options, an attacker can execute arbitrary code in the Node.js process; independently, a crafted deeply-nested object handed to `_.flatten` or `_.isEqual` can crash the process via stack exhaustion. Update underscore to >=1.13.8 and confirm no code path in the application passes attacker-controlled strings into `_.template`.
7: - `injection-eval-pretax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (preTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:32`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can submit a POST /contributions request with preTax set to arbitrary JavaScript (e.g. `require('child_process').execSync('id')` or a process-crashing payload) and have it executed in the Node process, giving full server-side code execution under the application's privileges. Never eval request data. Parse the value with Number()/parseInt() and reject non-numeric input, as the commented-out fix in the same file (lines 37-40) already shows.
8: - `injection-eval-aftertax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (afterTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:33`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting afterTax to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution. Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) plus a NaN check before use.
9: - `injection-eval-roth` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (roth) (`app/routes/contributions.js:34`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting roth to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution. Replace eval(req.body.roth) with Number(req.body.roth) or parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) plus a NaN check before use.
10: 
11: ### high
12: 
13: - `access-idor-allocations-userid` — Allocations route is an IDOR: any logged-in user can read any other user's allocation data by editing the URL (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, confirmed) — Any authenticated low-privilege user can walk the numeric :userId path segment (e.g. /allocations/1, /allocations/2, ...) and receive another user's stock/fund/bond allocation data. Ignore the :userId route parameter and load allocations for req.session.userId only, or verify req.session.userId === req.params.userId (or that the caller is admin) before calling the DAO.
14: - `access-missing-admin-check-benefits` — Admin-only benefits routes have no role check; any logged-in user can view and overwrite any other user's benefit start date (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, confirmed) — Any authenticated non-admin user can POST an arbitrary userId and benefitStartDate to overwrite another employee's benefits record, and can view the admin benefits roster of all non-admin users -- a full vertical privilege escalation on a state-changing route. Add the existing isAdmin middleware to both routes exactly as the commented-out code shows: app.get("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...) and app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...).
15: - `access-password-compare-not-constant-time` — Login compares passwords with plain string equality on plaintext-stored passwords instead of a constant-time hash verify (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-916, confirmed) — The === comparison leaks timing information proportional to the number of matching leading characters, letting an attacker who can measure response time recover a valid password character-by-character; independently, because passwords are stored in plaintext, any read access to the users collection discloses every user's real password in the clear, not a hash. Hash passwords on signup with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())) and verify with the library's constant-time bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password) instead of ===.
16: - `access-csrf-missing-profile-update` — No CSRF protection anywhere in the app: profile update (bank account, SSN, address) is forgeable from a cookie-authenticated session (`app/routes/index.js:48`, CWE-352, confirmed) — A page on another origin that auto-submits a form to POST /profile (the victim's session cookie is attached automatically by the browser) can silently overwrite the victim's bank account number, routing number, SSN, address, and name. 17: - `data-config-logged-at-startup` — Full application config, including session secret and crypto key, is dumped to stdout on every start (`config/config.js:12-13`, CWE-532, confirmed) — Anyone who can read the process's stdout/log files - container logs, a log-aggregation pipeline, a support engineer, or an attacker with log read access - obtains the session-signing secret, the crypto key, and the database credentials in one line, enough to forge sessions for any user and to connect to the database directly. Re-enable field-level encryption (AES-256-GCM with a random IV per record, key from a vault) before writing ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting, and decrypt only when displaying to the owning user.
19: - `data-cleartext-http-transport` — Application only listens over plain HTTP; TLS is fully disabled (`server.js:145`, CWE-319, confirmed) — Any attacker positioned on the network path (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP, or a man-in-the-middle) can read or modify login credentials, session cookies and all submitted PII in transit. Terminate TLS at the app or a reverse proxy in front of it, redirect all HTTP to HTTPS, and set the session cookie's `secure` flag once TLS is in place.

21: - `dependencies-body-parser-dos` — body-parser is pinned to a range that resolves to a version with two denial-of-service advisories (`package.json:9`, CWE-405, confirmed) — An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted request body to exhaust event-loop time or bypass the configured body-size limit, denying service to the whole application. Update body-parser to >=1.20.6 (within the declared ^1.15.1 range; npm audit reports a non-breaking fix is available) and regenerate the lockfile.
22: - `dependencies-marked-xss-redos` — marked is pinned to an exact, years-old version with active XSS and ReDoS advisories, and is wired into templates (`package.json:17`, CWE-79, confirmed) — A user who can submit markdown content (e.g. via the memos feature) can bypass marked's sanitize option and inject script that executes in another user's session, or trigger a ReDoS that stalls the single Node.js event loop for every request. 23: - `dependencies-mongodb-driver-outdated` — mongodb driver is pinned to an ancient 2.x range with a DoS advisory and an unmaintained transitive driver-core (`package.json:18`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — A malformed server response or crafted query result can crash or hang the database connection layer that every route in the application depends on; the 2.x driver also predates years of TLS, authentication and query-hardening fixes shipped in later majors. At minimum update to mongodb >=3.1.13 to clear the known DoS; plan a migration to a current major (7.x) since the 2.x line is long past any security support window.
24: - `injection-nosql-where-allocations` — NoSQL injection via unsanitized threshold in MongoDB $where clause (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`, CWE-943, confirmed) — An attacker can submit GET /allocations/<userId>?threshold=' ; while(true){} // or an operator such as 0' ; return true; var x='0 to run arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server, causing denial of service or bypassing the intended filter to read every user's allocation data. Validate and allowlist the destination host (e.g. restrict to finance.yahoo.com) before calling needle.get, resolve and re-check the IP to block private/link-local/metadata ranges, and never let the request supply the full request URL.
26: - `injection-xss-memos-marked` — Stored XSS: unescaped markdown-rendered memo output with autoescape disabled (`app/views/memos.html:31`, CWE-79, confirmed) — Any logged-in user can submit a memo containing HTML/script content (e.g. via a markdown construct marked's sanitizer fails to strip, or raw HTML since sanitize is not a full parser-level guarantee) that executes in every other user's browser when they view /memos, enabling session/cookie theft or actions performed as another user. - `injection-eval-pretax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (preTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:32`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can submit a POST /contributions request with preTax set to arbitrary JavaScript (e.g. `require('child_process').execSync('id')` or a process-crashing payload) and have it executed in the Node process, giving full server-side code execution under the application's privileges. Never eval request data. Parse the value with Number()/parseInt() and reject non-numeric input, as the commented-out fix in the same file (lines 37-40) already shows.

- `injection-eval-aftertax` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (afterTax) (`app/routes/contributions.js:33`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting afterTax to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution. Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) plus a NaN check before use.

- `injection-eval-roth` — Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution percentage (roth) (`app/routes/contributions.js:34`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server by setting roth to a malicious expression, achieving remote code execution.
